title: Quantile-driven geo routing with load shepherd and soft-eject circuit breakers
creator: Marcus Lee
description:
Goal: Implement a quantile-driven multi-region request router that preserves P95/P99 SLOs while maximizing successful throughput across regions. Introduce a lightweight "load shepherd" component that proactively steers and sheds traffic using short-lived capacity credits and a soft-eject circuit-breaker per region. Deliverables: routing policy, admission controller, per-region scoring, rollout plan, tests, and dashboards.

Context: Recent SEV-3 incidents showed region-wide latency spikes that cascaded to global latency SLO breaches because the router kept sending traffic to a stressed region until it fully degraded. Current binary geo-pin / fallback logic is brittle: it does not account for load shape, quantile degradation, or progressive shedding. This ticket designs and implements a finer-grained policy that: 1) routes based on quantile latency signals (p50/p95/p99) and available capacity tokens; 2) applies geo pinning with decay (sticky for short windows but automatically relaxes); 3) triggers soft-eject circuit breakers that move traffic incrementally away from unstable regions instead of full failover; 4) supports controlled shedding (by priority) at the edge to avoid system-wide collapse.
acceptance_criteria: Router uses p95 and p99 latency signals from region telemetry to compute region scores and route decisions in production traffic path
Load shepherd exposes a capacity credit counter per-region; router consults credits before routing to a region
Soft-eject circuit-breaker reduces traffic to a region in stages (25%, 50%, 75%) based on sustained quantile breaches and recovers automatically when signals improve
Geo pinning honors TTL decay and can be overridden by explicit routing policies (pin by customer or route)
Load-shedding path drops or queues only lower-priority requests and returns clear error codes and metrics (429/503 with reason tags)
End-to-end canary in staging, gradual rollout to 10%/50%/100% with health gating per-step
Dashboards show region score, credits, eject state, shed counts, and SLO burn rate; alerts fire when burn rate crosses threshold
design_notes:
Core idea: score each region every 10s using a combination of p50,p95,p99, success-rate, and available GPU queue depth. Compute a composite 'fidelity' score that biases latency-sensitive routes to low-p99 regions while allowing cost-sensitive routes to prefer cheaper regions. The load shepherd maintains a sliding window of admitted tokens representing sustainable QPS for the region. Tokens are refilled at a dynamic rate based on autoscaler signals and recent observed tail latency. When tail latency exceeds thresholds for configured windows, the circuit-breaker enters staged soft-ejects: reduce acceptance fraction by configured steps. Geo pinning attaches a short TTL (default 60s) to affinity; if region stays healthy, TTL extends with exponential backoff up to a max.

Data plane changes: add quick-check hook in the Router's admission flow: consult region_score and credits, then decide Accept / Delay (push to retry queue) / Shed. Control plane exposes tuning knobs: quantile thresholds, eject steps, credit refill formula, pin TTLs.

Telemetry: synthetic probes per-region (50 RPS of 1-2s synthetic requests) to supplement production quantiles during low-traffic windows. Use reservoir sampling for p99 to avoid bias from probe-only traffic.

Safety: default to conservative fallback policy (existing global fallback) if router control plane becomes unavailable.
tradeoffs:
- Aggressive quantile-based routing improves tail latency for latency-sensitive customers but may increase overall cost by routing more to larger capacity regions.
- Soft-ejects reduce blast radius vs full failover but add routing complexity and more frequent churn.
- Capacity credits add additional state and coordination; we keep state per-region with cheap counters to limit coordination surface.
- Synthetic probes help coverage but can skew p99 if not isolated; we use tagged metrics to separate probe vs production samples.
- Prioritized shedding prevents system collapse but requires accurate request priority labeling across SDKs (work for SDK team).
rollout_plan:
1) Implementation in staging with feature flag (router.v2.quantile_steering) and shepherd inactive by default. 2) Integration tests + scale test in perf env with 1M requests/hour synthetic workload. 3) Canary: enable on low-traffic tenant subset (10%), monitor metrics for 30m. 4) Progressive rollouts to 50% then 100% with 30m gating. 5) Post-rollout: keep conservative thresholds for 72h then tune.

Rollback: feature-flag off or revert to existing simple geo-pin fallback.
monitoring_and_alerting:
Dashboards: region_latency_quantiles, region_score, region_credit_balance, circuit_breaker_state, shed_rate_by_route, sLO_burn_rate_per_route.
Alerts: - region_score_drop: fires when a region_score drops below critical for >30s
- credit_depletion: when region_credit_balance < 5% for >10s
- unexpected_shed_spike: shed_rate increases >x compared to baseline
- slo_burn_high: route-level SLO burn rate > 10% over 5m (auto rollback trigger for canary)
All alerts include suggested runbook steps: check autoscaler, check kernel/gpu metrics, consider increasing soft-eject aggressiveness.
test_plan: Unit tests for scorer and credit refiller. Integration tests: simulated multi-region latency degradations and verify staged soft-eject behavior. Chaos tests: kill region process and validate circuit-breaker transitions and graceful shed. Load tests: ensure router QPS overhead <5% and credit operations scale to 10k regions in worst-case simulation. Canary smoke: verify that 95th percentile latency improves for latency-sensitive routes and that shed errors are confined to lower-priority routes.
